 Brazil Integrates Qdenga Dengue Vaccine into Public Health System Amid Epidemic Challenges

 Brazil Integrates Qdenga Dengue Vaccine into Public Health System Amid Epidemic Challenges
 Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on Linkedin Share on Reddit Share on Telegram 
 Following formal regulatory approval from the National Health Surveillance Agency, Brazil became the first country in the world to incorporate a dengue vaccine into its public health system, seeking to curb severe disease manifestations and alleviate acute pressures on hospital infrastructure. A critical commentary published in Discover Viruses analyzes the nationwide integration of the tetravalent Qdenga vaccine, designated TAK-003, across Brazil’s Unified Health System. The authors examine the epidemiological, logistical, and economic considerations shaping this immunization policy, which emerged in direct response to historically unprecedented arboviral transmission patterns across the Region of the Americas and within Brazilian municipalities specifically.
 Epidemiological surveillance records compiled for the Region of the Americas underscored the severity of the crisis, documenting more than 4.2 million reported dengue infections throughout 2023, which encompassed over 6,500 severe cases and 2,050 deaths. This caseload surpassed the previous regional threshold recorded in 2019 by more than one million cases. Across epidemiological weeks 1 through 49 of 2023, regional incidence stood at 421 cases per 100,000 inhabitants with an observed case fatality rate of 0.049 percent. Brazil reported the overwhelming majority of these infections, logging 2,909,404 individual cases, while Peru and Mexico registered 271,279 and 244,511 cases, respectively.
 The epidemiological burden accelerated further during the opening weeks of 2024, prompting numerous Brazilian states to declare public health emergencies before widespread vaccine deployment could begin. Within the first three weeks of January 2024 alone, Brazil’s Ministry of Health confirmed more than 120,000 dengue cases and at least 12 fatalities, a marked escalation compared to the 44,700 cases and 26 deaths documented during the equivalent timeframe in 2023. By April 2024, formal states of emergency had been instituted across nine federative units: Acre, Amapá, Distrito Federal, Espírito Santo, Goiás, Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro, Santa Catarina, and São Paulo. The highest incidence was concentrated among young adults aged 20 to 29 years, reaching 894 cases per 100,000 in men and 1,086 per 100,000 in women, while the most severe clinical complications were observed predominantly among individuals aged 80 years and older.
 Regulatory approval for Takeda Pharmaceutical’s Qdenga was authorized by the National Health Surveillance Agency in 2023 for individuals aged 4 to 60 years regardless of baseline serostatus. Clinical evidence from Phase 3 trials demonstrated that Qdenga conferred an overall cumulative efficacy of 83.6 percent against hospitalization caused by virologically confirmed dengue and 62.0 percent against virologically confirmed symptomatic infection within a trial cohort comprising both seropositive and seronegative participants. Qdenga is formulated as a live attenuated vaccine administered via subcutaneous injection in a two-dose schedule of 0.5 mL per dose, with an intended administration interval of 90 days between applications.
 Severe global manufacturing constraints immediately restricted the total volume of doses available for nationwide procurement, forcing federal authorities to establish targeted prioritization frameworks. While the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics identified approximately 13.6 million children and adolescents between 10 and 14 years of age across the country, initial manufacturer delivery guarantees could cover only 3.2 million individuals. The pharmaceutical supplier indicated that it could supply a total of 6.5 million doses throughout 2024, beginning with an initial delivery of 750,000 doses in January followed by 570,000 doses in February, with remaining shipments scheduled to arrive intermittently through November. Total annual delivery capacity was projected to expand to 9 million doses in 2025, alongside discussions between Takeda and the Butantan Institute to explore local manufacturing partnerships.
 To optimize the allocation of these restricted vaccine supplies, the Ministry of Health established rigorous geographic and demographic selection criteria in consultation with state and municipal leaders, the Technical Advisory Chamber on Immunization, and World Health Organization guidelines. Municipal eligibility required an urban population exceeding 100,000 inhabitants alongside elevated transmission rates across 2023 and 2024 and confirmed local circulation of dengue virus serotype 2, which is associated with dengue hemorrhagic fever. Historical assessments showed that 176 large municipalities had generated 48.2 percent of all probable dengue cases nationwide and 93.1 percent of probable cases within large urban centers between 2013 and 2022. The resulting rollout initially focused on children and adolescents aged 10 to 14 across 530 municipalities located within 16 states and the Federal District.
 Economic modeling highlighted significant financial benefits associated with incorporating TAK-003 into the Unified Health System. An assessment published by the National Commission for Technology Incorporation in 2023 estimated the total unit cost for complete two-dose vaccination at 371.28 Brazilian Reais, based on a procurement cost of 170.00 Reais per dose combined with logistical expenditures of four percent and anticipated operational wastage of five percent. This total intervention cost was approximately 92 percent lower than expenditures typically incurred by public health infrastructure for outpatient clinical management, inpatient hospitalization, and intensive care unit admissions for severe dengue manifestations, establishing a favorable overall cost-benefit balance for public health budgets.
 Clinical efficacy profiles revealed critical biological nuances, particularly regarding recipient serostatus and viral serotypes. Phase 3 trial evaluations demonstrated broad protection across all four dengue serotypes among individuals who had experienced prior dengue infection. In contrast, among dengue-naive individuals lacking prior viral exposure, the vaccine demonstrated limited protective efficacy, proving effective only against serotype 1 and serotype 2 while failing to demonstrate consistent protection against serotype 3 and serotype 4. Because Qdenga is a live attenuated formulation, it is strictly contraindicated during pregnancy and among immunosuppressed individuals suffering from underlying conditions or undergoing immunosuppressive treatments.
 Operational guidelines established that pre-vaccination diagnostic testing is unnecessary, permitting administration without prior proof of infection. However, individuals with recent laboratory-confirmed dengue infection are advised to wait six months before initiating the vaccination regimen. If natural infection occurs after receiving the primary dose, the secondary dose should proceed without resetting the schedule, provided it is administered at least 30 days after symptom onset. In February 2025, the Ministry of Health revised administrative guidance to authorize the temporary reallocation of doses nearing a two-month expiration window to new localities, while expanding recipient eligibility to ages 6 to 16. By late March 2025, national surveillance documented a 75 percent reduction in dengue notifications and an 83 percent reduction in related mortality compared to early 2024 figures, with vaccine availability expanding across 1,921 municipalities following the distribution of 930,000 supplementary doses.
 Despite documented epidemiological improvements, the commentary highlights significant remaining hurdles that necessitate sustained entomological and genomic surveillance. Continued vector control remains imperative to prevent the transmission of other arboviruses carried by Aedes mosquitoes, especially as individuals may perceive diminished personal risk following vaccination. Epidemiological tracking in 2025 revealed substantial shifts, with dengue virus serotype 3 accounting for more than 40 percent of circulating transmission cases in settings where vaccine coverage against this serotype remains limited. The Southeast region recorded 360,000 cases, with São Paulo reporting 285,000 probable cases and 168 of the 217 confirmed national fatalities. Furthermore, because current regulatory approval excludes adults over 60 years—the demographic experiencing the greatest severity and mortality—additional studies remain necessary to evaluate safety and clinical efficacy in older populations, while potential manufacturing collaborations and candidate vaccines, such as the Butantan vaccine anticipated for review in 2025, could support broader population coverage.
